title: What makes a Korean restaurant a 맛집?
excerpt: A word that tells you where to eat, and why Koreans love sharing good places.
photoAlt: Food stalls in a Korean market
question: What is your favourite local restaurant, and why would you recommend it?
paragraphs: If a Korean friend suggests visiting a 맛집 (matjip), you are probably about to eat something good. 맛 means flavour, and 집 literally means house. Together, the word describes a place known for serving good food.

A 맛집 can be a tiny family-run restaurant or a celebrated modern dining room. Recommendations often travel through friends, colleagues and online communities. A queue might catch your attention, but the real test is whether the food suits your own taste.

Gwangjang Market in Jongno is a fun place to try the idea for yourself. It is known for dishes such as 빈대떡 (mung bean pancakes), 꼬마김밥 (small seaweed rice rolls) and 떡볶이 (spicy rice cakes). Choose something you can share, then wander to another stall if you are still hungry.

When asking for a neighbourhood full of good food, try 맛집 골목이 어디예요? It means “Where is the alley with good restaurants?” If you have already found a restaurant, 추천 메뉴가 있나요? asks whether there is a recommended dish.

Next time you discover a place you love, tell a friend about it. That is part of the pleasure of finding a 맛집. The best recommendation is often a small story about what you ate and why you want to go back.

title: Why Seoul turns old factories into cafés
excerpt: A slow afternoon in Seongsu reveals a different side of the city.
photoAlt: Trees and pathways in Seoul Forest, near Seongsu
question: Do you have a neighbourhood where old and new buildings meet?
paragraphs: Walk east from Seoul Forest and the scenery begins to change. Trees give way to brick buildings, workshops and cafés with surprisingly high ceilings. Welcome to Seongsu-dong, a Seoul neighbourhood where industrial history is part of its charm.

Seongsu has long been associated with manufacturing and handmade shoes. As designers, restaurants and cafés moved into the area, many old spaces found new uses. You can still pass a working repair shop on your way to a carefully designed coffee bar.

There is no need to make a long checklist. Start at Seoul Forest, walk toward the café streets, and choose one place that makes you curious. A good afternoon can be as simple as a park, a cup of coffee and a few unexpected shops.
If you would rather keep walking with your drink, say 포장할게요. It means “I'll take it to go.” If you want to stay, you can say 먹고 갈게요, a common way to say you will eat or drink in.
One of Seoul's pleasures is discovering how much a neighbourhood can change within a few streets. Take your time and look up at the buildings as you walk.

title: The streets of Hongdae are a stage
excerpt: Follow the music through one of Seoul's most expressive neighbourhoods.
photoAlt: Street scene in the Hongdae neighbourhood of Seoul
question: What street performance has stayed in your memory?
paragraphs: On an evening in Hongdae, you might hear music before you can see the performance. A crowd gathers around a singer or a dance group, then disperses to another street. It is a lively way to encounter Seoul's creative culture.

The neighbourhood grew around Hongik University and has become associated with independent music, art, fashion and nightlife. Visit Seoul describes the R2 pedestrian area as a place for busking, where performers and passersby share the street.

You can enjoy Hongdae without buying a ticket or following a fixed itinerary. Browse a small shop, stop for a snack and spend a little time listening. Keep pathways clear and be considerate of other people enjoying the performance.
If you are exploring with a new friend, 사진 좀 찍어 주실래요? is a polite way to ask someone to take your photo. You can practise it before your next trip.
Hongdae changes with the time of day. A quiet afternoon can turn into an evening full of lights and music. Visit the neighbourhood at your own pace and see what catches your attention.

title: The smallest part of a Korean hello.
excerpt: A slight bow can say a lot before the conversation begins.
photoAlt: A narrow Seoul lane with shop signs and tiled eaves; contextual image, not a greeting demonstration
question: What small gesture makes a greeting feel warm where you live?
paragraphs: Imagine meeting a friend’s parent for the first time in Korea. You have practised your greeting, but suddenly there is another question: what should your body do? Before you can decide, they offer a small bow. The whole movement takes less time than your carefully rehearsed sentence.

In many everyday greetings, a Korean bow can be a slight dip of the head and upper body. It accompanies the words rather than stopping the conversation for a ceremony. Think of it as a quiet way to acknowledge the person in front of you.

The setting matters. A greeting to an older person or someone in a senior role may be more formal than one between close friends. There is no single movement that fits every relationship. For an ordinary introduction, a small, unhurried bow gives you a place to start; you can take your cue from the people around you.

Try pairing that first introduction with 만나서 반가워요. It means “Nice to meet you.” Say it slowly enough to enjoy saying it. You are welcoming a person into a conversation, so leave a little space for their name and their reply.

Sometimes a handshake follows. If the other person offers one, you can use your right hand and lightly support it with your left. You do not need to rush through a bow and a handshake at the same moment. A brief pause makes room to notice what the other person is doing.

Bows can also appear when people say goodbye. Once you start noticing them, the interesting part is how small some are: a short movement that helps close an encounter. You do not need to greet every passerby or turn each interaction into a formal occasion.

On your next introduction, give your hello a little room. Put the phone down, notice the person and let the words arrive with the movement. What small gesture makes a greeting feel warm where you live?

title: One coffee. Your first little win in Korean.
excerpt: You do not need a perfect sentence to order your usual.
question: What would you like to order in Korean?
paragraphs: You reach the counter. You know what you want. Then the menu, the queue and the thought of getting the words wrong arrive all at once. A small sentence helps: 아메리카노 한 잔, 주세요. One americano, please.

The useful part is 주세요, juseyo. It makes a request polite and gives you a starting point you can reuse. You are asking for something, not delivering a speech. A pause or a second try is completely fine.

Listen once at a comfortable speed. Say the sentence without the audio. Then listen again and notice where the words run together. That small comparison is more useful than trying to memorise every sound perfectly at once.

At the cafe, the next question might be about the size, temperature or whether you are staying. It is all right to point at the menu or ask for a moment. This phrase is the beginning of a conversation, not a promise that you will understand every reply.
Try it today, even if today’s cafe is your kitchen. Tomorrow, come back and see whether the sentence arrives a little more easily.

title: A phone on the table. Where did its owner go?
excerpt: A small cafe moment opens a bigger conversation about trust.
question: What surprises you most about cafes in Korea?
paragraphs: In some Seoul cafes you may notice a laptop, a bag or a phone on a table while its owner is briefly away. For visitors used to carrying everything even to the bathroom, it can be an unexpectedly memorable detail.
Sometimes the person is ordering. Sometimes they have stepped away for a moment. An object can also signal that a seat is taken. It is an informal habit, not a written rule shared by every cafe.

The interesting question is not whether every belonging is safe. No place can promise that. It is how people interpret the same small scene: one visitor sees a risk, another sees a seat being held, and someone else barely notices.
If you are visiting, choose the level of care you are comfortable with and keep passports, valuables and essential belongings with you. You can enjoy noticing a custom without having to copy it.
And if a busy cafe’s seating system is unclear, ask the staff before settling in. The best cultural discoveries often start with a simple question.

title: The New Year arrives in a bowl.
excerpt: Why tteokguk belongs at the Seollal table.
photoAlt: Gyeongbokgung Palace in Seoul; context image
question: Which food feels like a new beginning to you?
paragraphs: A holiday can announce itself through a sound, a journey or a smell from the kitchen. During Seollal, Korea’s Lunar New Year, one familiar sign is a bowl of tteokguk: soup with sliced rice cakes.

Eating it on New Year’s morning carries a traditional connection with becoming a year older. The expression is part of the holiday’s story. A bowl of soup does not change your official birthday or age.

Rice cake soup is only one part of the table. Depending on the household, you may also see pancakes, dumplings or other dishes prepared for sharing. There is no single meal that represents every family.

For a visitor, the useful lesson is to leave a little room in the plan. A holiday can change opening hours and the rhythm of a neighbourhood. Check the places you want to visit rather than assuming an ordinary weekday schedule.
You do not need to know every tradition to enjoy learning about it. Start with a bowl, a question and the stories people choose to tell you.
author: Korea 101 by Sori

title: In Busan, choose the kind of day before the places.
excerpt: A beach morning and a hillside afternoon need room between them.
question: Sea views or little streets: what is your kind of afternoon?
paragraphs: A list can make every place in a city look equally close. A map quickly tells a different story. In Busan, the beach districts around Haeundae and Gwangalli and the older downtown around Nampo belong to different parts of the day.

Try choosing a mood first. A coastal day might leave time for the beach and a cafe. A downtown day might bring together markets and a neighbourhood walk. You do not have to collect every landmark to feel that you have been somewhere.

Gamcheon’s hillside lanes ask for a different pace from a flat promenade. It is also a residential neighbourhood. Follow visitor routes, keep your voice down and allow time for slopes, stairs and transport.

Put your hotel on the map before adding the third or fourth stop. The journey back is part of the plan, too. Compare actual transport options in your map app rather than judging a trip only by a straight line.
Then invite a friend. Sometimes the most useful part of a shared itinerary is discovering that both of you would rather sit with a view for another half hour.
author: Korea 101 by Sori

title: Your first Korean journey starts before the city.
excerpt: A hotel pin can make an airport arrival feel a little less complicated.
question: What makes arriving in a new country easier for you?
paragraphs: There is a particular feeling to arriving in a new country: excitement, tiredness and a phone full of information you suddenly need at the same time. Before choosing what to visit, save where you are sleeping.

If you arrive at Incheon, choose the correct terminal. AREX connects the airport with Seoul, and the all-stop service connects at places including Hongik University and Gimpo. An express train to Seoul Station is not automatically the most convenient option for every hotel.

Gimpo has airport rail and Metro 5 and 9 connections. For Busan’s Gimhae Airport, light rail connects with Metro 2 at Sasang and Metro 3 at Daejeo. The last connection to your accommodation still matters.

Schedules, luggage, accessibility and how you feel can all change the best choice. Open current directions and compare a train connection with other options. A static travel tip cannot promise a live departure.
Once the first journey is settled, the city feels a little more manageable. The cafes and beautiful streets can wait until you have put down the bag.
